title: Labor squeeze prompts revised construction workforce strategies
excerpt: During webinars from ABC and AGC this month, firms talked about ramping up investment in training and workforce development.
content_html:
Sebastian Obando

Mon, September 14, 2026 at 4:03 AM CDT 5 min read

This story was originally published on Construction Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily Construction Dive newsletter.

A softer construction market hasn't made qualified workers much easier to hire.

For the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, more contractors slashed staffing numbers than added workers over the past year, said Ken Simonson, chief economist at Associated General Contractors of America, during a Sept. 3 webinar about labor supply.

"This is the first year since we came out of the pandemic that we saw more firms reducing than increasing headcount," said Simonson. "In other words, while some firms are adjusting to weaker demand, many contractors continue to compete for limited supply of qualified workers."

Indeed, 87% of firms still report openings for craft workers, according to a workforce survey from AGC and the National Center for Construction Education and Research. Among those firms with openings, 88% of respondents said filling them was as difficult or harder than a year ago.

The disconnect is pushing contractors to other strategies in addition to recruitment.

"You cannot hire your way out of this situation," said Mindy Bates, human resources director at Ace Electric, a Valdosta, Georgia-based electrical contractor, during the AGC webinar. "We got to grow it from within as well."

Develop talent already in the building

New research points to multiskilling, or training craft workers to perform complementary tasks, as another possible solution, according to a study released by the Simplar Foundation and faculty from Arizona State University, University of Kansas and the University of North Carolina at Charlotte.

The study estimated that for every 10 multiskilled workers observed, between 14 and 17 single-trade workers would be needed to cover the same scope of work, said Brian Lines, an associate professor in the civil, environmental and architectural engineering department at the University of Kansas, during ABC's Sept. 2 live event.

But that trust to handoff tasks needs to be properly won, said Lines.

"The definition of multiskilling we're using here is that it's a workforce strategy where workers are qualified to perform selected tasks safely and competently across more than one trade, craft or skill classification," said Lines. "Now, this does not mean that individual workers are performing informal task switching. Doesn't mean that every worker is performing every task."

For workers, additional skills can open paths to career advancement too, said Joel Dutton, preconstruction manager at Evans General Contractors, during the ABC session. Dutton started his construction career as a welder before his employer sent him to a training program to develop new skills.
